newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Africa more attractive to investors - SBC Warburg.
newsitem.headline: Africa more attractive to investors - SBC Warburg.

text.p: Africa is becoming an increasingly attractive investment destination for funds who previously shied away from a continent perceived to be a high risk, SBC Warburg corporate finance division director Michael Spriggs said on Wednesday.
Speaking at the opening of a three-day Investing in Africa Mining conference, Spriggs said investment flows to Africa had previously been hampered by perceptions of risk.
But the strong growth in Western money supply in recent years "provides the basis for a surge in international investment", particularly to high growth emerging markets, he said.
"For funds looking for diversified portfolios, Africa now has increasing attractions," Spriggs said.

"To invest in Africa does present a number of risks. It is not for the faint hearted...but the combination of reasonably strong economic growth, low interest rates, growing international fund liquidity (make it attractive)," he added.
Other speakers stressed that political stability and investor friendly regimes were vital to unlock the vast and diverse mineral wealth on the continent.
London-based mining and financial consultant David Williamson said in a keynote address that the rest of Africa was moving closer to South Africa, which until now dominated African mining.
"The rest of Africa is starting to catch up," he said.
Williamson said the countries likely to emerge over the next few years as key players with exciting potential in Africa could be split into two categories.

The first consisted of countries that already had a moderately well developed mining industry and were likely to keep on improving. These included Botswana, Namibia, Tanzania, Zaire, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
"Zaire is included purely from a geological/prospectivity point of view, since if the political situation cannot be resolved, then obviously its mining potential can never flourish," he said.
The second category included Chad, Eritrea, Mali and Senegal.

"All these countries have highly prospective terrain which is likely to host a whole range of mineral/metal deposits, yet due to their lack of development, they remain for the most part unexplored," Williamson said.
All were also moderately stable countries and had recently revised their mining codes to make themselves more attractive to foreign investors. -- Lynda Loxton, Cape Town newsroom, +27-21 25-2238
